name: Air polishing (Airflow)

lead: Air polishing sprays water, air and fine powder at the teeth to lift surface stain and soft plaque. People in appearance circles get it for coffee, tea, wine and tobacco marks, without scraping, so teeth look lighter and cleaner right after.

The powder jet abrades away extrinsic stain and biofilm. It changes surface colour, not the tooth's own shade, which is what peroxide bleaching targets. Research on the technique centres on gum and implant maintenance rather than cosmetics.

paras: It is done by a dentist or hygienist, usually during a cleaning visit. Powders include sodium bicarbonate, glycine and erythritol, with lower-abrasion powders studied for use around gums and implants.

Reported cautions include contraindications for people on sodium-restricted diets or with hypertension, respiratory or kidney conditions, possible gum or surface effects, and aerosol generation during the procedure.

web.title: Air polishing: we've come a long way, baby - Today's RDH

chain: Coffee, tea and wine marks removed
angle.text: A dentist's powder-jet cleaning lifts coffee, tea, wine and tobacco stain from the surface, so teeth look lighter right after the visit. It does not change the tooth's own shade, which is what bleaching does.

lead: Air polishing, often called by the brand-derived name Airflow or described as powder-jet polishing, is a dental procedure in which a handpiece sprays a pressurised mix of water, air and fine powder onto the teeth to remove extrinsic stains and soft deposits such as plaque biofilm. It is performed by dentists and hygienists, usually during a cleaning visit, and people use it to lift coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco staining and brighten the visible surface of the teeth without scraping.[1][2]

Dental sources place it within the broader practice of tooth polishing, whose purposes are to remove extrinsic stain and plaque, improve aesthetics and smooth restorations, and which Wikipedia describes as having little therapeutic value on its own.[1] The traditional powder is sodium bicarbonate; lower-abrasion powders such as glycine and erythritol were developed so the jet can be used below the gumline and around implants.[3][4][5]

Air polishing changes the colour of the tooth surface by removing stain, rather than changing the intrinsic shade of the tooth, which is what peroxide whitening targets.[2] Published research on the technique is concentrated on periodontal and implant maintenance, with trials comparing it to scaling and to rubber-cup polishing; cosmetic outcomes are described mainly in textbooks and clinical commentary.[1][5][6][7]
infobox: Rubber-cup polishing with paste, bristle brush

paras: A powder jet handpiece delivers warm water, compressed air and a fine abrasive or non-abrasive powder in a stream directed at the tooth surface. Wikipedia describes the older version as a prophy-jet spraying water and sodium bicarbonate that works well on extrinsic stains and soft deposits.[1]

Staining commonly comes from coffee, tea, red wine, smoking, chromogenic bacteria in plaque, some antimicrobial rinses and exposure to metallic dust, and polishing in general is used to remove it.[1] The more familiar alternative is polishing with a rubber cup or bristle brush and polishing paste on a prophylaxis angle, with dental tape for the surfaces between teeth.[1]

As a cosmetic step, air polishing is used for stain removal at hygiene visits and before or alongside whitening, because surface stain can hide the underlying tooth shade.[1][2] Because the jet reaches grooves and between-tooth areas that a rotating cup can miss, practitioners describe it as efficient for stained surfaces.[1]

Some clinics package the powder jet inside a staged cleaning workflow that begins with a plaque-disclosing stain, then uses air polishing and an ultrasonic scaler. In a 2024 randomised split-mouth trial in 60 periodontitis patients treated by dental students, this guided biofilm therapy protocol and a conventional protocol with hand instruments and rotary polishing produced comparably good clinical results.[8]

Lower-abrasivity powders were developed so that the jet can be used below the gumline. A 2010 randomised split-mouth trial of 50 maintenance patients with residual pockets applied glycine powder subgingivally with a disposable nozzle. No adverse events were noted, patients rated it as less painful than hand instrumentation and it was quicker, although it was not microbiologically superior to scaling and root planing.[9] Reviews have discussed subgingival air polishing for periodontal biofilm infections.[5]
Systematic reviews have examined air polishing as an adjunct for peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, the inflammatory conditions around dental implants.[6][3]

Wikipedia notes that tooth polishing dates back to Roman and Greek times and credits Pierre Fauchard, the father of modern dentistry, with introducing polishing to remove stains, using early pastes made from substances such as ground coral, eggshell, ginger or salt.[1] Polishing was routine for all patients before the 1970s, and from the 1990s and 2000s evidence led many institutions to recommend selective polishing based on whether stain is present.[1]

Air abrasion polishing with sodium bicarbonate began as a stain-removal tool. A dental hygienist writing in Today's RDH in 2018 describes the older bicarbonate units as messy and salty, and notes that coarse powders of around 64 micrometres or more were reported to wear root surfaces and soft tissue.[10] Finer glycine powder of about 25 micrometres, used below the gumline, became available from around 2004, a subgingival nozzle was presented at EuroPerio 6 in 2009, and a still finer erythritol powder of about 14 micrometres reached the European market in 2013, according to the same account.[10] The author says the finer powders need an air polisher calibrated for them.[10]

Manufacturers and some clinics now package the jet into a staged protocol, often marketed as guided biofilm therapy: a disclosing agent shows where plaque and stain are, air polishing removes the biofilm and stain, and scaling follows only where needed.[10][8] The hygienist's account describes patients noticing a cleaner feel and a sweeter taste and observing pinker, less bleeding gums, but those outcome claims come from her own clinic experience rather than from the studies she cites.[10]

A routine dental cleaning, as described on Wikipedia, comprises scaling to remove plaque and tartar and polishing, with debridement when heavy calculus has built up.[11] Polishing, including air polishing, removes some plaque and stain but not calculus, so it is done together with scaling and not in place of it.[11] Because the jet works on stain and soft deposits and the whitening gels used for bleaching work on the colour inside the tooth, hygienists often discuss the two as complementary steps: stain is cleared first, so the true shade shows before any bleaching.[2][1]

Published human research on air polishing is mostly clinical-periodontal rather than cosmetic. A systematic review of five studies found glycine-powder air polishing as effective as control treatments at peri-implant mucositis sites, with a larger reduction in bleeding on probing at peri-implantitis sites (a weighted mean difference of about 24 percentage points favouring air polishing), although complete disease resolution was uncommon.[3][3] A larger meta-analysis of 32 studies likewise reported bleeding reductions favouring glycine-powder air polishing and Er:YAG laser for non-surgical peri-implantitis treatment.[6]

A 12-month randomised trial in 43 patients with peri-implantitis found that adding erythritol air polishing to conventional instrumentation did not produce added clinical benefit, and that the test group reported more pain or discomfort, particularly among women.[12] A consensus report on peri-implant disease covers non-surgical treatment and maintenance.[13]

Registered trials include comparisons of trehalose versus glycine powder in peri-implant mucositis,[14] erythritol air polishing in peri-implantitis,[15] and a trial comparing bristle brush, rubber cup and air polishing for tooth surface roughness after scaling.[7] Several are recruiting or unreported.

Wikipedia lists contraindications for sodium bicarbonate air polishing including sodium-restricted diets, hypertension, respiratory illness, infectious disease, chronic kidney disease, Addison's or Cushing's disease, and use of mineralocorticoids, antidiuretics or potassium supplements.[1] Other precautions cover teeth without stain, newly erupted teeth, demineralised areas, exposed root surfaces, sensitivity and gum inflammation.[1]

General polishing risks it describes include removal of the fluoride-rich outer enamel layer (which saliva and fluoride pastes can help remineralise), frictional heat, scratching of restorations and gum trauma from poor technique or powder forced below the gumline.[1]

A systematic review of 83 studies found that dental procedures generate droplets and aerosol, and placed air polishing in a higher contamination-risk tier alongside ultrasonic scaling and high-speed handpieces; the authors cautioned that heterogeneity limited the conclusions.[16]
